text_blocks.snippet: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) occurs when the tiny arteries in your lungs thicken, narrow, or block. This makes it hard for blood to flow and forces the right side of your heart to work much harder.
snippet_highlighted_words: hard for blood to flow and forces the right side of your heart to work much harder

text_blocks.snippet: In the early stages, you may notice no symptoms at all. As the disease progresses, common signs include:

list.snippet: Shortness of breath: Especially during physical activity or exertion (such as climbing stairs or walking).
Fatigue and weakness: Feeling unusually tired because the heart and body lack proper oxygen.
Chest pressure or pain: Caused by the overworked and strained heart muscle.
Dizziness or lightheadedness: Often triggered during or after physical exertion.
Fainting (syncope): Occurs as heart strain and blood flow issues become more severe.
Heart palpitations or rapid pulse: Feeling your heart race, pound, or beat irregularly.
Swelling (edema): Fluid buildup causing swollen ankles, legs, or a bloated abdomen (as blood backs up into the liver and kidneys).
Bluish or gray lips and skin (cyanosis): A sign of low oxygen levels in the blood.

text_blocks.snippet: For detailed guidance on testing and management, you can review resources provided by the American Lung Association or the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
